an0417.user: Ok I need to talk this out before I lose it. We're a salon chain, doing about ₹36L a month, and on paper everything's fine — last 90 days the unit economics on our YouTube push are genuinely healthy, I'm not bleeding money. Is that a problem or am I just being paranoid because it's working?
an0417.assistant:
You're not paranoid, and the fact that the economics are healthy is exactly what's hiding the danger. The number that matters here isn't your CAC or your ROAS — it's the 94%. Roughly ₹34L of your ₹36L monthly revenue depends on one channel you don't own and can't control.

This isn't a performance problem, so don't go optimising the YouTube campaigns. It's concentration risk. One algorithm change, one ad-account suspension, one CPM spike during festive season, and you don't lose 10% — you lose half your business in a week, with no second engine to catch you. Healthy unit economics on a single fragile channel is still a single point of failure.

The lever: start a real second channel now, while it's a choice and not an emergency. Not a token ₹10K test you forget about — a genuine effort (local Google, WhatsApp retention on your existing client base, referral) funded and staffed enough to matter. The goal over the next two quarters is to get that 6% to 20-25%, so a bad month on YouTube is a dent, not a death.

Caveat: I can't tell you which second channel is right without seeing where your customers actually come from offline. But the direction is firm — diversify before you're forced to.

an0418.user: Running a D2C eyewear brand, mostly SEO and organic driving traffic. Last 30 days: AOV ₹1,700, gross margin 28%, CAC ₹876, ROAS sitting at 1.9, CTR around 1.4%. I've been reading up and I think my CAC is too high. How do I lower my CAC?
an0418.assistant:
Before you touch CAC, let's do the one piece of arithmetic that reframes this whole question. Contribution per order = ₹1,700 × 28% − ₹876 = ₹476 − ₹876 = −₹400. You lose ₹400 on every single order before a rupee of overhead, and that's true even if your ads are perfect.

So lowering CAC isn't the cure here. Say you're a hero and cut CAC by ₹150 — you're still at −₹250 an order. The 28% gross margin is the disease; the ad cost is just the symptom you happened to notice. No targeting tweak, no keyword negative, no creative refresh fixes a margin this thin, because the problem lives in your COGS and your price, not your marketing.

The lever: rework your unit economics before your ad strategy. Push AOV (bundles, lens upgrades, a second frame), renegotiate COGS, or raise price — get gross margin toward 50%+ where ₹876 of CAC can actually be absorbed. At 50% margin that same order contributes ₹850 − ₹876 = roughly breakeven, and now CAC optimisation actually means something.

Caveat: 28% is unusually thin for eyewear, where frames often carry strong margins — so first sanity-check the number itself. If it's real, that's where the work is, not in the ad account.

an0422.user: I'm pulling my hair out. D2C pet-care, growth mostly through SEO and organic but we've been pushing paid hard alongside it. Over the last 8 weeks I scaled spend from ₹5L to ₹9.5L and instead of growing, my efficiency tanked — ROAS went from 3.0 down to 1.8, CAC climbed from ₹597 to ₹993. AOV ₹1,800, margin 62%. an0422.assistant:
What's happening is the most predictable thing in paid growth, and it's not a failure on your part — you hit the channel's ceiling. Walk the numbers: you nearly doubled spend (₹5L → ₹9.5L) and ROAS fell almost exactly in proportion (3.0 → 1.8) while CAC went from ₹597 to ₹993. That symmetry is the signature of saturation, not a broken account.

The mechanism: your first ₹5L was buying your best, highest-intent audiences — the people most likely to convert, the cheapest to reach. When you forced another ₹4.5L through the same channel and the same audiences, there were no more cheap high-intent buyers left. The extra budget went to colder, pricier reach, so every incremental order cost more and the blended numbers sagged. You didn't do anything wrong; you exhausted a finite pool.

The good news in your favour: contribution is still healthy — ₹1,800 × 62% − ₹993 = ₹1,116 − ₹993 = +₹123 even at the worse CAC, so you're not bleeding, you're just buying growth inefficiently.

The lever: create new demand before adding more budget. New audiences, new creative angles, a second channel — give the spend somewhere fresh to go instead of pushing harder into a tapped-out pool. Caveat: 8 weeks of a clean trend is a real signal, so trust this read — but confirm the saturation by checking whether frequency climbed alongside CAC.

an0423.user: Salon chain here, testing Amazon Ads for our product line. Last 30 days: 780,000 impressions, 11,661 clicks so CTR about 1.5%, but only 109 orders. AOV ₹1,150. Running broad-match keywords. The reach looks great but the orders aren't there — what's the non-obvious thing I'm missing?
an0423.assistant:
Your CTR is fine — 1.5% is perfectly normal, so stop looking there. The number that tells the real story is downstream: 109 orders from 11,661 clicks is a 0.93% conversion rate. Out of every hundred people who clicked your ad, fewer than one bought. That's not a creative problem; that's an intent problem.

The mechanism is sitting in one phrase you mentioned: broad-match keywords. Broad match shovels you huge volume — that's your 780K impressions and healthy click count — but it pulls in people loosely browsing, searching adjacent terms, comparison-window-shopping. They click because the ad caught their eye, then bounce because they were never in a buying mindset for your product. You're paying for traffic, not customers. Optimising CTR further just buys you more of the wrong people.

The lever: tighten intent. Move the budget toward exact and phrase match on high-intent buying terms, mine your search-term report and add the junk queries as negative keywords, and stop letting broad match define who sees you. Fewer, better-qualified clicks will lift that 0.93% far more than any headline tweak.

Caveat: a single 30-day window with only 109 orders is a directional read, not gospel — but the conversion gap is wide enough that intent mismatch is the clear suspect. Pull the search-term report first; it'll show you exactly which queries are wasting spend.

an0424.user: Going slightly mad here. HR-tech SaaS, spent ₹15L on ads last 30 days post-iOS. My ad platform dashboard says ROAS is 3.6. My Shopify last-click report says ROAS is 1.4. Same period, same spend, two completely different numbers. One of these is lying to me and I can't tell which one to trust or what to actually do. Help.
an0424.assistant:
Neither one is lying, and that's the part you have to make peace with. They're measuring two different things, and both are biased — the truth sits somewhere between 1.4 and 3.6, not at either end.

The platform's 3.6 uses modelled conversions and a 7-day-click attribution window, and it has every incentive to credit itself generously — post-iOS it's partly estimating conversions it can no longer see directly. Shopify's last-click 1.4 only credits the very final touch before purchase, so it systematically under-counts every ad that started or assisted a journey that closed elsewhere. One over-claims, one under-claims. You will never get these two dashboards to agree, because they're built on opposite assumptions. Refereeing them is a waste of your energy.

The lever: stop treating either platform ROAS as absolute truth and anchor on blended CAC instead. Take total spend across everything ÷ actual new customers (count real new logos in Shopify), and manage the business to that one number over time. It's attribution-agnostic — it doesn't care which dashboard claims credit, it just tells you what a customer truly cost you.

Caveat: blended CAC is cleanest when you're not running heavy brand or offline spend muddying the new-customer count — so make sure the customers you divide by are genuinely new, not renewals or organic that happened to land in the window.

The trap here is real and common: founders react to one noisy week, yank the levers, and end up whipsawing the account — which actually does create instability, so the next bad week feels like proof they were right to panic. You'd be manufacturing the problem you're afraid of.

Do nothing yet. Let it run. A real signal looks like the same direction holding for 3-4 consecutive weeks, or a single move big enough to clearly clear the noise band — not a one-week 17% blip on 89 conversions. Until you see that, there's nothing to diagnose and nothing to fix.
